note.text: A comparison needs a purpose and criteria. Distance, cost, travel time, accessibility and the nature of a load can affect a choice. One means of transport is not automatically best for every journey. Use comparatives with a clear basis and qualify claims when evidence is limited. The original passage presents conditions for discussion; it does not supply current fares or route availability.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: A comparison needs a purpose and criteria. Distance, cost, travel time, accessibility and the nature of a load can affect a choice. One means of transport is not automatically best for every journey. Use comparatives with a clear basis and qualify claims when evidence is limited. The original passage presents conditions for discussion; it does not supply current fares or route availability.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Original passage: An imaginary club must carry bulky displays to a nearby hall. Walking suits members carrying light personal bags, but the bulky items need suitable arranged transport. A distant journey raises different questions about time, cost and access. The club checks the actual conditions before choosing rather than assuming that the fastest option on one route is best everywhere.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify the traveller's goal and constraints. Compare the same feature across alternatives and explain a trade-off. Avoid unsupported universal claims such as buses are always fastest. State what further information would be needed for a real decision.
